info.bio:
Marshall Bruce Mathers III (St Joseph, Misuri, 17 de octubre de 1972), conocido por su nombre artístico Eminem (estilizado EMINƎM) y también por su álter ego Slim Shady, es un rapero, productor discográfico y actor estadounidense. Su nombre artístico proviene de la unión de las iniciales de Marshall Mathers: M&M («Em and Em», estilizándose como Eminem).

Eminem es el artista con más ventas de la década de 2000 en los Estados Unidos. A lo largo de su carrera

scenes.name: 50 Cent, G-Unit y las mixtapes
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Las mixtapes venían de las cintas de Herc, Flash y los Cold Crush, y en Nueva York las firmaban Kid Capri, Ron G, DJ Clue o Tony Touch. Curtis Jackson, apadrinado por Jam Master Jay y presentado por él a Sha Money XL, provocó con «How to Rob» (1999), donde planeaba atracar a las estrellas; tras «Ghetto Qu’ran» le dispararon nueve veces (2000) y Columbia lo despidió. Con Sha Money inundó la calle de mixtapes robando bases ajenas: sobrevivir lo convirtió en la historia. Guess Who’s Back? (2002) convenció a Eminem, que lo fichó con Dr. Dre (Shady/Aftermath): Get Rich or Die Tryin’ (2003) e «In da Club» devolvieron el gangsta al gran público como no se veía desde Death Row. Todos copiaron su modelo (DJ Drama, detenido en 2007 por sus Gangsta Grillz). G-Unit dejó escapar a J. Cole, que fichó por Jay-Z.
scenes.family: Nueva York: Def Jam, Queens y la edad de oro

scenes.name: Eminem, Esham y el Detroit de las batallas
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Esham, influido por los Geto Boys y el punk, retrató en Boomin’ Words from Hell (1989) el Detroit del crack y de la Devil’s Night: el «acid rap» («un puñetazo en la cara alegre») y un sello independiente, Reel Life. Marshall Mathers, amigo de Proof en el circuito de batallas, fracasó con Infinite (1996, F.B.T. y Web Entertainment); despedido de cocinero, recorrió el país compitiendo: segundo en la Scribble Jam de Cincinnati (1997), donde venció a Rhymefest con una rima sobre la raza que el público aplaudió; Rhymefest obligó a Wendy Day a escuchar su maqueta y ella lo llevó a sus Rap Olympics de Los Ángeles, donde perdió ante Otherwize pero ganó la visita a The Wake Up Show de Sway & King Tech: allí lo oyó Dr. Dre, que lo fichó para Aftermath/Interscope. Un rapero blanco que superó las acusaciones de apropiación y abrió paso a Mac Miller o Logic.
scenes.family: Otras escenas: Filadelfia, el Medio Oeste, Virginia

scenes.name: Grammys, Óscars, Hall of Fame y el Pulitzer
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: Los grandes premios rechazaron o reconocieron tarde al hip hop. En los Grammy de 1984, la noche de Thriller, Herbie Hancock tocó «Rockit» con Grand Mixer D.ST en los platos: para Paradise Gray, la primera vez que se vio en la tele. En 1989 se creó el Grammy al mejor rap pero se entregó fuera de la retransmisión: Def Jam y Rush encabezaron el boicot y DJ Jazzy Jeff & the Fresh Prince no fueron a recoger el premio por «Parents Just Don’t Understand»; Kool Moe Dee sí fue, harto de que nadie hablara de estrategia («¿no decíamos que nos importaba un carajo el Grammy?»). En 1990 Young MC lo ganó en directo a «Fight the Power» y Flavor Flav le asaltó el escenario. Eminem fue el primer rapero en ganar un Óscar con «Lose Yourself» (2003, con Luis Resto), y Three 6 Mafia el segundo; Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five entraron los primeros en el Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (2007). En 2014 Macklemore se disculpó con Kendrick Lamar por ganarle; en 2018 DAMN. de Lamar, criado en Top Dawg por Punch, ganó el Pulitzer, algo que Nation of Millions habría merecido treinta años antes.

scenes.name: Rap y hip hop
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: A finales de los ochenta el «rockero» es una figura tan obsoleta como lo fue el cantante pop en 1956: tres revoluciones toman la música popular (el DJ como fuerza creativa, el hip hop y la fusión ciberpunk de industrial, metal y hardcore). En 1975 Kool Herc reinventa el breakbeat en el Bronx; el rap es una evolución del dub jamaicano. Sugar Hill Gang, Kurtis Blow, los «mensajes» de Grandmaster Flash, Afrika Bambaataa (el Leonardo del beatbox, inventor del «electro»), el tocadiscos como instrumento, Run-DMC, Tackhead, L.L. Cool J, Eric B & Rakim y Public Enemy (It Takes A Nation Of Millions, la obra maestra del hip hop). El gangsta rap (Schoolly D, NWA, Ice Cube, Dr Dre, 2Pac), Beastie Boys, las raperas (MC Lyte, Queen Latifah), De La Soul, A Tribe Called Quest, Cypress Hill; en Gran Bretaña, Art Of Noise.
scenes.family: Soul, funk, disco, hip hop y baile

scenes.name: Was (Not Was) y Don Was
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: Donald Fagenson y David Weiss, amigos de infancia de Oak Park, mezclaron rock, funk y jazz en «Wheel Me Out» (Ze, 1980), éxito en Gran Bretaña y sintonía oficiosa de los DJs de Direct Drive. Su debut en Island (1981, con Marcus Belgrave) siguió el linaje disco; Born to Laugh at Tornadoes (Geffen, 1983), lleno de sintetizadores, cajas Linn y vocoders, juntó a Mel Tormé, Mitch Ryder y Ozzy Osbourne. Como Orbit, Don Was hizo «The Beat Goes On», su respuesta a «Tour de France» sobre un tema de Sonny & Cher, con sintetizadores de Luis Resto (luego Oscar con Eminem), y produjo a Felix and Jarvis. Su talento para lo paradójico dio filo al sonido de Detroit y lo separó del disco y del house de Chicago.
scenes.family: Detroit antes del techno: clubes sociales y fiestas de instituto

scenes.name: Hip hop
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: La cultura del sound system jamaicano llega a Nueva York: un ritmo repetitivo y roto aislado de los breaks del funk, y el DJ convertido en héroe.
scenes.family: Hip hop, breaks y ritmo lento

scenes.name: R&B
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: El pop de chicas y el soul actualizados con producción electrónica y síncopas de hip hop; en su flanco experimental se emparenta con la IDM y el dancehall.
scenes.family: Hip hop, breaks y ritmo lento

podcast.title: Debut Album Release (November 1996)
podcast.body: Eminem released his debut album, _Infinite_, in November 1996, preceding his appearance on the Warped Tour in 1997, where he was still working to gain recognition. "He just released a debut album, the previous November, and was still trying to get anybody to pay attention to him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Participant in 1997 Tour
podcast.body: Eminem, described as a "white rapper from Detroit," was on the Warped Tour in 1997, actively trying to garner attention for his music. "And also this white rapper from Detroit named Eminem."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Career - Pre-1999 Releases
podcast.body: Before his breakout success with *The Slim Shady LP* in 1999, Eminem had been active since the mid-90s, releasing singles and an earlier album in 1996. This period laid the groundwork for his later mainstream recognition. "No era su primer trabajo llevaba desde mitad de los 90 publicando ya ciertos singles incluso tenemos un disco anterior de 1996."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Illuminati Clone Conspiracy Theory (2000)
podcast.body: A conspiracy theory, originating in AOL chatrooms around 2000, suggests that Eminem died in a car accident on December 15, 2000. According to this theory, the Eminem seen today is a clone created by "super scientists" of the Illuminati. "There's a conspiracy theory that's been circulating since the days of AOL chatrooms in 2000 that M&M actually died in a car accident on December 15, 2000."

podcast.title: Target of Mariah Carey's "Obsessed" (2009)
podcast.body: Eminem, who had been "rapping shady things about Carey for years," became the target of Mariah Carey's 2009 hit "Obsessed." This marked an instance of a pop/R&B singer openly dissing a rapper, showcasing the evolving landscape of diss tracks across genres. "Mariah Carey even scored a hit openly dissing an actual rapper M&M, who had been rapping shady things about Carey for years."

podcast.body: Eminem maintained a distinctive aggressive and furious flow throughout his career, which was highly innovative and fresh. This style, while present in earlier rap, was perceived as lost in the 90s among wealthy "black rappers," but Eminem brought it back with a unique intensity. "Nunca ha perdido esa manera de hacer su flow tan rabiosa y tan furiosa que yo creo que fue muy novedosa."

podcast.body: Eminem is cited as an artist who has incorporated backward messages into his music, a practice that experienced a resurgence with the advent of digital sound editing software in the late 1990s and early 2000s. "Back, cake, cold play, M&M, Fransford Nand, Lincoln Park, Marilyn Manson, Moby Soundgarden Tool, 21 Pilots, and a ton more."

podcast.body: Eminem, "the top-selling rapper of the Aughts," largely "built his career on disses," frequently "concocting imagined beefs with other celebrities." This strategy was evident in songs like "The Real Slim Shady" and "Without Me," which targeted numerous public figures. "And the top-selling rapper of the Aughts, Eminem, essentially built his career on Diss'es, concocting imagined beefs with other celebrities."

podcast.title: Dual Persona - Slim Shady vs. Marshall Mathers
podcast.body: Eminem presented two distinct characters: the irreverent, disrespectful, and commercially critical rapper known as Slim Shady, who focused on "irreverent rap," and the serious rapper, Marshall Mathers, who made "true rap." His albums often blended both aspects. "Tenemos dos personajes muy distintos uno es el Eminem tan irreverente y respectuoso que se mete tanto con la cultura comercial y que a lo mejor no es un atanto a rap serio y es un atanto más a rap irreverente lo que él llama con la personalidad de Slim Shadey y por el otro lado tenemos a Eminem de verdad o a Marshall que es ese rapero serio que hace verdadero rap."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Elton John as AA Sponsor
podcast.body: Elton John serves as Eminem's sponsor for Alcoholics Anonymous. Eminem reaches out to Elton John for strength whenever he needs it, knowing that Elton profoundly understands addiction. "Whenever M. feels that he needs strength, he calls Elton, who of course understands addiction all too well."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Enduring Anger - Wealth vs. Lyrical Content
podcast.body: Despite becoming incredibly wealthy and established, Eminem has remarkably retained his "furious and enraged flow," expressing anger at a world that made his early life difficult. This consistency in his message allows many people to continue identifying with him. "Aunque Eminem ha ganado mucho dinero y es una persona increíblemente rica y asentada en cierto modo no ha perdido ese carácter de flow tan rabioso y tan furioso enfadado con un mundo que le hizo una vida difícil al principio."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Evolution Beyond Slim Shady - From Irreverent to Serious
podcast.body: As the "prefabricated consumer culture" of the late 90s and early 2000s faded, Eminem gradually shed his Slim Shady persona, which became less socially relevant. He increasingly focused on more serious, professional, and "old school" rap, appealing more to critics and genuine rap followers. "Eminem poco a poco se ha ido desprendiendo de ese personaje de Slim Shady porque posiblemente socialmente ya había perdido gran parte de su contenido o de su sentido porque la sociedad en la que había nacido ese personaje había evolucionado."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Evolving Lyrical Themes - Personal and Social Issues
podcast.body: Eminem's lyrics are incredibly evolutionary, delving deeply into real-world problems that extended beyond the racial minority issues often discussed in social rap. He tackled personal struggles like problems with his daughter, issues with an alcoholic mother, and themes of aggression towards his wife, making his content relatable to a broader audience. "Eminem hablaban de problemas con lluvales de sus problemas por ejemplo de criar a su hija de los problemas que tuvo con una madral cólica de problemas agresividad por ejemplo las canciones de vía mi mujer como otro y no sé si matarlo no porque me siento rabioso."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: False Media Association with Michael Miller Murders
podcast.body: In 2009, when Michael Miller committed a stabbing spree against his family, the media erroneously reported that he was screaming lyrics from an Eminem song, specifically "Here comes Satan, I am the Antichrist, I am going to kill you." The transcript explicitly clarifies that "there is no such M&M song with those lyrics," indicating a misattribution by the media. "Weirdly though, there is no such M&M song with those lyrics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Featured in Apple Commercials
podcast.body: Eminem's music has been showcased in Apple commercials, highlighting the company's use of influential artists across various genres to appeal to a broad audience for products like the iPod and iPhone.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 2

podcast.title: Guantanamo Bay Torture
podcast.body: Ruha Al-Ahmad, a Bangladeshi captured in Afghanistan in 2001 and sent to Camp Delta at Guantanamo Bay, was subjected to hours and hours of Eminem on full blast during interrogations. At one point, he endured this for 20 straight hours, as authorities sought information about alleged terrorist connections. "To get him to talk, he was subjected to hours and hours and hours of Eminem on full blast."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Identification with White Youth - Anti-Establishment Voice
podcast.body: Eminem resonated with many young people who felt alienated by the pre-fabricated, ridiculous pop music of the late 90s and early 2000s, such as the Spice Girls, Backstreet Boys, and Britney Spears. He voiced the frustrations and criticisms that many adolescents felt towards mainstream culture, speaking to "normal people from the street" who didn't identify with those commercial products. "Venía Eminem hablar precisamente de lo que yo creo que todos estábamos pensando de aquella, todos los adolescentes pensábamos que todo eso empezaba a ser lamentable."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Lyrical Revolution - Bringing Black Rap to White Culture
podcast.body: Eminem uniquely took the discourses of classic "black rap" out of their original context and introduced them to the world of mass white consumption, embedding them within established, commercial white culture. He applied the same defiant and aggressive attitude, normally associated with "black cultures," to white societal issues, which was perceived as shocking and groundbreaking. "Él sacaba de contexto todas esos discursos del rap clásico negro para meterlo en el mundo del gran consumo de blanco lo metían dentro de la cultura blanca más asentada y más comercial."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Music for Working Out
podcast.body: Eminem's music was identified as among the best for working out, alongside Michael Jackson and Queen, according to a stationary bikes manufacturer. "The best music for working out... Michael Jackson, Eminem, and Queen."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Own Clothing Brand
podcast.body: Eminem is cited as one of the many artists who now possess their own clothing brand, a business strategy popularized by the Wu-Tang Clan. "Jason, Kanye West, Eminem, Nas, todos tienen su premio, marca de ropa."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Prominent Solo Rapper
podcast.body: Eminem is cited as an example of a prominent solo rapper, distinguishing him from larger groups or "clans" in hip hop. "Tenemos tipos de raperos, tenemos el rapero en solitario, como en Eminem"

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Wu Tang Clan. Historia viva del Hip Hop

podcast.title: Relatable Realities - Addressing White Working-Class Struggles
podcast.body: Eminem’s music resonated with a reality often ignored by mainstream media, which portrayed an idealized "white culture of success" through shows like *Friends* or *Sex and the City*. He voiced the anger and frustration of white people from structured families, living in difficult circumstances in places like Detroit, who faced everyday problems that "black rap" didn't directly address. "Venir a alguien que había formado parte de eso y que tenía esa rabia interna y esa furia interna de rechaza a la sociedad que tenía Eminem porque lo había vivido y eso yo creo que mucha gente de esta cultura blanca se sintiese identificada con él."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Ringtone Popularity - Mid-2000s
podcast.body: In the mid-2000s, songs by artists like Eminem were constantly heard as ringtones in public spaces such as the subway, schools, hospitals, and streets. This reflected a widespread desire among young people to publicly display their musical tastes and individuality. "Canciones de Metallica, Eminem, Fifth Dissent, Blint Note, Linkin Park, The Vanessens, sonaban constantemente en el metro, en el colegio, en el hospital, en la calle."

podcast.title: Songs About Jeffrey Dahmer
podcast.body: Eminem is among the numerous artists mentioned who have written songs about the serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer. "Jeffrey Dahmer seems to have the most songs written about him with about 50 Pearl Jam, Slayer, Black Eyed Peas, Katy Perry, Eminem, Dr. Dre, Violent Femmes, J. Cole and many more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Slim Shady Persona - Irreverent Agitator
podcast.body: Eminem initially appeared with the image of an agitator, grotesque, critical, ill-mannered, and disrespectful. This persona, known as Slim Shady, featured an aggressive and furious flow coupled with critical and acidic lyrics that pushed rap into new, previously unexplored territory. "Eminem aparecía con ese look o con esa imagen de agitador, de grotesco, de crítico, de mal educado, de faltón."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Zero DB Initiative Signatory
podcast.body: Eminem is among the artists who signed the Zero DB initiative, formed in 2008 as part of the charity Reprieve. This initiative encourages condemnation of music as torture and advocates for governments to enforce the Convention Against Torture. "The Sinees include Tom Morello, average against the machine, members of REM, rise against Pearl Jam, Trent Reznor, Limp Biscuit, system of a down, disturbed the estate of Prince, the Chili Peppers, Eminem, Marilyn Manson, Neil Diamond, Dr. Dre, and a host of others."

xref.title: Guantanamo Bay Torture
xref.body: Music by Dr. Dre was used as a form of musical torture at Camp Delta, Guantanamo Bay. Prisoners, including Ruha Al-Ahmad, were forced to listen to it, sometimes while wearing headphones, for extended periods. "If it wasn't Eminem, the music came from Dr. Dre and Meatloaf, sometimes while being forced to wear headphones."

xref.title: Guantanamo Bay Torture
xref.body: Meat Loaf's music was among the tracks used for musical torture at Camp Delta, the military prison at Guantanamo Bay. Prisoners were sometimes forced to listen to it, even through headphones, for extended periods during interrogation. "If it wasn't Eminem, the music came from Dr. Dre and Meatloaf, sometimes while being forced to wear headphones."

xref.title: Matt Helders' Drummer Origin
xref.body: Matt Helders became the band's drummer by necessity, as all other instruments were already claimed, making him the "Ringo" of the group. His background included being "very much into beats" and listening to Motown due to his parents' influence. By his teens, he was deeply immersed in hip hop, with Wu Tang, Outcast, and Eminem as favorites, and he harbored dreams of becoming a DJ by age 14.
